prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Barack Obama reached out to Iran on Friday -- the start of the Iranian New Year -- in a video message offering "the promise of a new beginning" that is "grounded in mutual respect." Obama's message to Iran echoes his inaugural speech, where he said "we seek a new way forward." The message is a dramatic shift in tone from that of the Bush administration, which included Iran, along with North Korea and Iraq, in an "axis of evil." It also echoes Obama's inaugural speech, in which he said to the Muslim world, "we seek a new way forward, based on mutual interest and mutual respect." In Friday's video, Obama said: "The United States wants the Islamic Republic of Iran to take its rightful place in the community of nations. You have that right, but it comes with real responsibilities. And that place cannot be reached through terror or arms, but rather through peaceful actions that demonstrate the true greatness of the Iranian people and civilization." There was no immediate response from Tehran to Obama's message, but Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad said last month that his country would welcome talks with the United States "in a fair atmosphere with mutual respect." The United States, several European nations and Israel suspect that Tehran has been trying to acquire the capacity to build nuclear weapons, but Iran says its nuclear program is solely for peaceful purposes. Last month, the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security released a report saying that Iran has reached "nuclear weapons breakout capability" -- it has enough uranium to make a nuclear bomb. The report was based on an analysis of data from the International Atomic Energy Agency. However, an IAEA official who asked not to be named cautioned against drawing such dramatic conclusions from the data, saying Iran's stock of low-enriched uranium would have to be turned into highly enriched uranium to be weapons-grade material. That hasn't been done, the official said. The United States has had tortuous relations with Tehran since the Islamic revolution in 1979, but the Obama message speaks of "new beginnings" with the promise of a new year. "We have serious differences that have grown over time. My administration is now committed to diplomacy that addresses the full range of issues before us, and to pursuing constructive ties among the United States, Iran and the international community," the president said. "This process will not be advanced by threats. We seek, instead, engagement that is honest and grounded in mutual respect."

WASHINGTON (CNN) — President Barack Obama reached out to Iran on Friday—the start of the Iranian New Year—with a video message offering “the promise of a new beginning” grounded in “mutual respect.”

Obama’s message to Iran echoed his inaugural address, in which he said, “we seek a new way forward.” It also marked a dramatic shift in tone from the Bush administration, which had included Iran, along with North Korea and Iraq, in an “axis of evil.” In that same inaugural speech, Obama told the Muslim world that “we seek a new way forward, based on mutual interest and mutual respect.”

In Friday’s video, Obama said: “The United States wants the Islamic Republic of Iran to take its rightful place in the community of nations. You have that right, but it comes with real responsibilities. And that place cannot be reached through terror or arms, but rather through peaceful actions that demonstrate the true greatness of the Iranian people and civilization.”

There was no immediate response from Tehran to Obama’s message. However, Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad said last month that his country would welcome talks with the United States “in a fair atmosphere with mutual respect.”

The United States, several European nations, and Israel suspect that Tehran has been trying to acquire the capacity to build nuclear weapons. Iran, however, maintains that its nuclear program is intended solely for peaceful purposes.

Last month, the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security released a report stating that Iran had reached “nuclear weapons breakout capability”—meaning it had enough uranium to make a nuclear bomb. The report was based on an analysis of data from the International Atomic Energy Agency.

However, an IAEA official, who asked not to be named, cautioned against drawing such dramatic conclusions from the data. The official said Iran’s stockpile of low-enriched uranium would have to be converted into highly enriched uranium to qualify as weapons-grade material. That has not been done, the official said.

The United States has had tortuous relations with Tehran since the Islamic Revolution in 1979, but Obama’s message invoked the idea of “new beginnings” alongside the promise of a new year.

“We have serious differences that have grown over time. My administration is now committed to diplomacy that addresses the full range of issues before us, and to pursuing constructive ties among the United States, Iran and the international community,” the president said. “This process will not be advanced by threats. We seek, instead, engagement that is honest and grounded in mutual respect.”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — On Friday, coinciding with the beginning of the Iranian New Year, President Barack Obama addressed Iran in a video statement, extending what he described as “the promise of a new beginning” based on “mutual respect.”

The appeal reflected themes from Obama’s inaugural address, in which he said the United States was looking for “a new way forward.” It also marked a major change in tone from the Bush administration, which had grouped Iran with North Korea and Iraq as part of an “axis of evil.” In that inaugural speech, Obama had also told the Muslim world that “we seek a new way forward, based on mutual interest and mutual respect.”

In the video released Friday, Obama said the United States wants “the Islamic Republic of Iran to take its rightful place in the community of nations.” He added that Iran has that right, but that it also carries “real responsibilities.” Such a position, he said, cannot be achieved “through terror or arms,” but through peaceful conduct that reflects “the true greatness of the Iranian people and civilization.”

Tehran did not immediately issue a response to Obama’s remarks. However, Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad said the previous month that Iran would be open to discussions with the United States if they took place “in a fair atmosphere with mutual respect.”

The United States, Israel and several European countries believe Iran may be working to develop the capability to produce nuclear weapons. Iran, however, maintains that its nuclear activities are intended only for peaceful use.

The month before Obama’s message, the Institute for Science and International Security, based in Washington, published a report stating that Iran had achieved “nuclear weapons breakout capability,” meaning it possessed enough uranium to build a nuclear bomb. The report relied on an examination of information from the International Atomic Energy Agency.

But an IAEA official, speaking on condition of anonymity, warned against interpreting the data in such sweeping terms. The official said Iran’s supply of low-enriched uranium would first need to be converted into highly enriched uranium before it could be used as weapons-grade material, and that this had not occurred.

Relations between Washington and Tehran have been strained and difficult since Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution. Still, Obama’s message invoked the idea of “new beginnings” alongside the symbolism of a new year.

“We have serious differences that have grown over time,” Obama said. He stated that his administration was now committed to diplomacy covering the full range of issues between the countries and to seeking productive relations among the United States, Iran and the wider international community.

“This process will not be advanced by threats,” he said. “We seek, instead, engagement that is honest and grounded in mutual respect.”

In the message, Obama emphasized that any future engagement should be grounded in mutual respect and a willingness to move beyond decades of mistrust.

The outreach represented a significant change in tone from the previous U.S. administration. Under President George W. Bush, Iran had been labeled part of an “axis of evil,” a phrase that contributed to deep hostility between Washington and Tehran. By contrast, Obama’s message suggested a readiness to pursue diplomacy and to open a new chapter if Iran was willing to respond constructively.

Obama stated that Iran has a rightful place in the community of nations, acknowledging the country’s history, culture, and importance. However, he also made clear that this place comes with responsibilities. He said Iran must demonstrate its intentions through peaceful actions, rather than through support for terror or the pursuit of arms that could threaten other nations.

The message came after Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad had indicated that Iran would welcome talks with the United States, provided they took place in a fair atmosphere based on mutual respect. That statement suggested a possible opening for dialogue, though major disagreements between the two countries remained unresolved.

Among the most serious points of tension was Iran’s nuclear program. The United States and its allies have long suspected Iran of seeking the capability to develop nuclear weapons. Iran, however, has consistently insisted that its nuclear activities are intended solely for peaceful purposes, such as energy production and scientific development. Obama’s message therefore signaled a diplomatic overture, but also underscored that improved relations would depend on Iran addressing international concerns through peaceful and responsible conduct.

President Barack Obama used a video message marking the Iranian New Year, Nowruz, to offer Iran a “new beginning” in its relationship with the United States, signaling a sharp shift in tone from the confrontational approach that had defined much of the Bush administration’s policy toward Tehran.

In the message, Obama spoke directly to the Iranian people and to Iran’s leaders, saying the United States was prepared to pursue engagement grounded in “mutual respect.” He acknowledged the long history and cultural richness of Iran and suggested that future relations need not be defined by decades of mistrust, sanctions, and hostility.

“My administration is now committed to diplomacy that addresses the full range of issues before us,” Obama said in the address. He emphasized that the United States sought a relationship based not on threats, but on honest dialogue and shared interests. At the same time, he made clear that Iran would be expected to meet its international responsibilities.

The message represented one of the most visible early signs of Obama’s intention to change the direction of American foreign policy in the Middle East. Under President George W. Bush, Iran had been labeled part of an “axis of evil,” and Washington had often relied on pressure, isolation, and warnings over Iran’s nuclear activities and its role in the region. Obama’s outreach suggested a willingness to test whether diplomacy could achieve progress where confrontation had produced few results.

The gesture came amid continuing international concern over Iran’s nuclear program. Tehran has long insisted that its nuclear activities are intended for peaceful purposes, including energy production and medical research. The United States and several of its allies, however, have worried that Iran could use its nuclear infrastructure to develop weapons capability.

Assessments of Iran’s intentions and progress have remained disputed. Some intelligence findings have suggested that Iran halted aspects of a nuclear weapons program years earlier, while other officials and analysts have warned that its uranium enrichment activities could eventually give it the ability to build a bomb if it chose to do so. These uncertainties have made the issue a central source of tension between Iran, the United States, and the broader international community.

Obama’s Nowruz message did not resolve those concerns, but it reframed the way Washington appeared prepared to address them. Rather than beginning with threats or demands alone, the administration signaled that it wanted to open a diplomatic channel and explore whether direct engagement could reduce mistrust.

The outreach was also aimed at a broader audience inside Iran. By choosing Nowruz, a holiday associated with renewal and fresh starts, Obama sought to connect his diplomatic message with a moment of cultural significance. His words were carefully crafted to show respect for Iran’s people while still addressing the conduct of its government.

Whether Iran’s leaders would respond positively remained uncertain. Relations between the two countries had been strained since the 1979 Islamic Revolution and the hostage crisis at the U.S. Embassy in Tehran. Since then, disputes over sanctions, regional influence, support for armed groups, and nuclear development have repeatedly blocked attempts at rapprochement.

Still, Obama’s message marked an important symbolic opening. It suggested that the United States was prepared to move beyond the language of confrontation and pursue a more flexible strategy, one that combined pressure with the possibility of negotiation.

At a time when concerns over Iran’s nuclear ambitions continued to raise the risk of deeper conflict, the offer of dialogue underscored the administration’s belief that renewed communication could help reduce tensions and perhaps create the conditions for a more stable relationship.

**Obama offers Iran “new beginning” in Nowruz message**

WASHINGTON — President Barack Obama appealed directly to Iran’s leaders and people in a video message marking Nowruz, the Persian New Year, saying the United States is prepared to seek a “new beginning” in relations with Tehran if Iran chooses engagement over confrontation.

In the message, released by the White House, Obama said his administration was committed to diplomacy “grounded in mutual respect,” a phrase meant to signal a shift from the sharper rhetoric that defined much of the U.S.-Iran relationship during the Bush administration.

“My administration is now committed to diplomacy that addresses the full range of issues before us,” Obama said, adding that the process “will not be advanced by threats” but through “honest and constructive” engagement.

The outreach was one of Obama’s most direct efforts early in his presidency to open a channel with Iran, a country that has had no formal diplomatic relations with the United States since 1980. The message was timed to Nowruz, an important holiday in Iran and across the Persian-speaking world, and was addressed not only to the Iranian government but also to ordinary Iranians.

Obama acknowledged Iran’s history and culture, saying the United States recognized the contributions of the Iranian people. But he also made clear that improved relations would depend on Tehran’s choices.

“The United States wants the Islamic Republic of Iran to take its rightful place in the community of nations,” Obama said. “You have that right — but it comes with real responsibilities.”

U.S.-Iran relations have been frozen for nearly three decades, beginning with the 1979 Islamic Revolution and the seizure of the U.S. Embassy in Tehran, where 52 Americans were held hostage for 444 days. Since then, the two countries have clashed over a range of issues, including Iran’s support for militant groups, its role in Iraq and the broader Middle East, and its human rights record.

At the center of recent tensions is Iran’s nuclear program. Tehran says its nuclear activities are intended for peaceful energy and medical purposes. The United States and several allies have long suspected Iran is seeking the capability to build nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran denies.

The United Nations Security Council has imposed multiple rounds of sanctions on Iran over its refusal to suspend uranium enrichment, a process that can produce fuel for civilian reactors but, at higher levels, can also be used in nuclear weapons. Iran has insisted it has a right to enrich uranium under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Obama’s message appeared designed to offer Iran a diplomatic path while preserving pressure over the nuclear issue. The administration has said it wants to work with international partners to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, but Obama has also emphasized that direct diplomacy should be part of that effort.

The tone marked a contrast with former President George W. Bush, who labeled Iran part of an “axis of evil” in 2002. While the Bush administration also supported limited diplomatic efforts involving European negotiators, relations remained deeply strained throughout his presidency.

Iranian officials have often dismissed U.S. overtures as insincere, arguing that Washington must change its policies, including sanctions and support for Israel, before relations can improve. It was not immediately clear how Iran’s leadership would respond to Obama’s message.

Still, the video represented a symbolic opening at a moment when the new administration was attempting to recalibrate U.S. foreign policy. By speaking directly to Iranians during one of their most significant holidays, Obama sought to frame diplomacy not as a concession, but as a possible break from decades of mistrust.

“This is a season of new beginnings,” Obama said. “I would like to speak clearly to Iran’s leaders: We have serious differences that have grown over time. My administration is committed to addressing those differences through diplomacy.”

WASHINGTON — President Barack Obama used the start of the Iranian New Year to appeal directly to Iran’s people and leaders, offering what he called a chance for “a new beginning” in relations between Washington and Tehran after three decades of hostility.

In a videotaped message marking Nowruz, the Persian New Year, Obama said the United States wanted engagement with Iran based on mutual respect, while making clear that Tehran would have to address international concerns about its nuclear program and its role in the region.

“My administration is now committed to diplomacy that addresses the full range of issues before us, and to pursuing constructive ties among the United States, Iran and the international community,” Obama said.

“This process will not be advanced by threats,” he added. “We seek instead engagement that is honest and grounded in mutual respect.”

The message was notable not only for its conciliatory tone but also for Obama’s direct reference to the country’s official name, the “Islamic Republic of Iran,” a formulation seen by some analysts as a signal that Washington was not seeking regime change. Obama said Iran’s leaders faced a choice: “This is about the future we want for all our children. It’s about the responsibility we have to one another as human beings.”

He also said Iran’s “rightful place in the community of nations” could not be achieved through “terror or arms,” but through peaceful actions that demonstrate the “true greatness of the Iranian people and civilization.”

The White House released the message at the opening of Nowruz, a holiday celebrated in Iran and across parts of Central Asia, the Caucasus and the Middle East. The address represented one of the clearest early signs of Obama’s desire to shift U.S. policy toward Iran from isolation and pressure alone to a combination of diplomacy and incentives.

There was no immediate formal response from Tehran. Iranian officials have in the past dismissed U.S. overtures as insufficient unless accompanied by concrete policy changes, including an easing of sanctions and recognition of Iran’s regional role. Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad had often argued that Washington’s tone might change while its objectives remained the same.

Relations between the United States and Iran have been severed since the aftermath of the 1979 Islamic Revolution and the seizure of the U.S. Embassy in Tehran. Since then, the two governments have clashed over Iran’s support for militant groups, its opposition to Israel, U.S. military presence in the Gulf, and, most prominently, Iran’s nuclear program.

Western governments suspect Iran of seeking the capability to build nuclear weapons, a charge Tehran denies. Iran says its nuclear activities are for peaceful purposes, including electricity generation and medical research, and insists it has the right to enrich uranium under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

The United Nations Security Council has imposed multiple rounds of sanctions on Iran over its refusal to suspend uranium enrichment. The International Atomic Energy Agency has also reported unresolved questions about possible military dimensions of Iran’s nuclear work, while acknowledging that inspectors have continued to monitor declared nuclear facilities.

Obama’s message suggested that diplomacy could offer Iran a path out of isolation. “The United States wants the Islamic Republic of Iran to take its rightful place in the community of nations,” he said. “You have that right — but it comes with real responsibilities.”

The outreach marked a sharp contrast with the rhetoric of the Bush administration, which included Iran in an “axis of evil” and repeatedly warned of the dangers of Tehran’s nuclear ambitions. Still, Obama’s remarks also reflected continuity in U.S. demands: Iran would have to reassure the world that its nuclear program is peaceful and comply with international obligations.

Whether the message would lead to meaningful talks remained unclear. Analysts said the appeal could resonate with many Iranians who favor better ties with the West, but any diplomatic opening would depend on Iran’s top leadership, where deep suspicion of U.S. intentions remains entrenched.
